It is extremely fast, requiring only one lookup into the 2D opacity map per voxel [S1].

The claim states that the technique is extremely fast and requires only one lookup into the 2D opacity map per voxel. The provided text explicitly supports this in two places: 1) In the notes section, it lists 'Extremely fast segmentation: requires only one lookup into the 2D opacity map per voxel.' 2) In the main text under section 2.2, it explains that because the method operates on the transfer function domain rather than reprocessing all voxels explicitly, the update time is well below 0.25 seconds. The specific phrase 'requires only one lookup into the 2D opacity map per voxel' is present in the source material.

STF is a one- or more-dimensional transfer function where spatial information is used to derive the color, whereas statistical (and/or spatial) information is used to setup the opacity [S1].

The claim is a direct paraphrase of the definition provided in Source [S1]. The source explicitly states: 'In general, we say that a spatialized transfer function is a one- or more-dimensional transfer function, where spatial information has been used to derive the color, whereas statistical (and/or spatial information) is used to setup the opacity.' This matches the claim word-for-word in terms of the logical structure and the specific attributes assigned to color and opacity derivation.
supported
*   **Barycenter** $b(s,t)$: The centroid of the spatial positions [S1].

The claim states that the barycenter $b(s,t)$ is the centroid of the spatial positions. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines the barycenter with the formula $b(s,t) = 1/n * sum(pi)$, where $pi$ are the normalized positions of the contributing voxels. In geometry, the average of a set of points is the centroid. Therefore, the evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
The color is derived from spatial proximity in the histogram [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'spatial information has been used to derive the color' and describes a method where entries in the transfer function (histogram) are classified into groups based on spatial proximity (using a feature radius and spatial correspondence norm). Each group is then assigned a unique color. Therefore, the claim that the color is derived from spatial proximity in the histogram is fully supported by the text.

Unlike explicit segmentation which is time-consuming and not suitable for quick first impressions, STF performs segmentation on the transfer function domain automatically and fast, allowing interactive exploration [S1].

The claim states that STF performs segmentation on the transfer function domain automatically and fast, unlike explicit segmentation which is time-consuming, allowing interactive exploration. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Using the described spatialization of a transfer function we effectively perform a segmentation on the domain of the transfer function. The main advantage of this approach is that we do not need to perform an explicit time-consuming segmentation of the volume domain.' It further notes that 'If the feature radius is changed interactively we only need to reclassify all entries in the transfer function... the total update time including a redraw of the volume is well below a quarter of a second.' Additionally, Section 2.3 is titled 'Interactive Exploration' and describes pointing and clicking to select classes. Thus, every part of the claim is directly supported by the text.
supported

Steps: 1) Determine the scalar range for each class in the transfer function. 2) Attenuate the emission of each class using a linear ramp over its determined scalar range, decreasing emission for the lowest occurring scalar values. 3) For selected classes, attenuate emission linearly to create a shaded appearance [S1].

The claim describes the 'Pseudo-Shading' technique detailed in Section 2.4 of the source text. The source explicitly states: 'In the context of the STF we implement pseudo-shading by first determining the scalar range of each class. The we attenuate the emission of each class using a linear ramp over its scalar range.' It further explains that for selected classes, emission is attenuated linearly to create a shaded appearance (simulating a head-light). All steps mentioned in the claim are directly supported by the text.
supported
A technique to enhance feature discrimination by simulating a head-light appearance [S1].

The claim states that a technique enhances feature discrimination by simulating a head-light appearance. Source [S1], specifically in Section 2.4 titled 'Pseudo-Shading', explicitly states: 'In order to enhance the discrimination of features... This effectively simulates the appearance of a head light.' It further explains that this is achieved by attenuating emission at low scalar values to darken object silhouettes. Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim.
supported
It darkens object silhouettes by attenuating emission at low scalar values, making accumulated opacity predominant [S1].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Section 2.4 'Pseudo-Shading'. The text states: 'If we decrease the emission for the lowest occurring scalar values of the object, the features silhouette is rendered dark, since the accumulated opacity becomes predominant over the emission.' This matches the claim's description of darkening silhouettes by attenuating emission at low scalar values to make accumulated opacity predominant.
